newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers resume talks, protests worsen.
newsitem.headline: French truckers resume talks, protests worsen.

text.p: Striking French truck drivers resumed marathon negotiations with employers on Monday after tightening their eight-day-old stranglehold on the country's roads in the most serious labour unrest this year.

Roger Poletti, spokesman for the Workers Force (FO) trade union, said as the talks began that the number of roadblocks had risen to 180 from 136 earlier in the day, with tens of thousands of trucks blockading motorways, borders and fuel depots.
FO leader Marc Blondel met Transport Minister Bernard Pons and threatened to extend the strike to rail and air transport unless a deal was reached by Tuesday.
"What I can say very clearly is that if there is not a result by tomorrow morning, Workers Force will examine the conditions for extending the movement to transport," Blondel told reporters.

The Communist-led CGT called on its members to widen the action with a national day of demonstrations and solidarity rallies at the roadblocks on Wednesday, and five rail unions urged their members to support the strikes "with the appropriate means".

Truckers blocked Channel ports and German border crossings and tightened their noose on oil refineries and fuel depots after all-night negotiations ended in deadlock at breakfast time on Monday over their demands for higher wages, shorter hours and retirement at 55 rather than 60.
Conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe renewed his appeal for a deal to end the strike that is slowly squeezing the French economy and provoking friction with France's neighbours.

"I'm following the talks hour by hour," he said before the latest round of talks chaired by government mediator Robert Cros. "The government has done everything to get these talks under way. They must now resume and finish."

A German truck driver became the first serious casualty of the strike on Monday when French truckers pelted his lorry with stones at a roadblock near Chalon-sur-Saone in eastern France. The driver from the Stuttgart region, whose name was witheld, suffered head wounds and underwent emergency surgery in Dijon.
The unrest showed signs of spreading to other sectors.

The major CFDT union called for a 48-hour strike of crew at state-owned airline Air France on Wednesday and Thursday, and for a 24-hour strike at state-owned utilities Electricite de France and Gaz de France on December 3.
The dispute is the most serious unrest since a 24-day round of public sector strikes against the centre-right government almost paralysed the country late last year.

Buoyed by an opinion poll showing 74 percent public support, truckers tightened blockades of refineries and oil depots, stopping lorries from using the Channel ports of Calais and Boulogne and frontier crossings with Germany in Alsace.

They let cars and buses embark on Channel ferries but stopped trucks. A port spokesman in Calais said British truck drivers joined the action in sympathy for about an hour, disrupting ferry loadings for cars.

The action added to the woes of travellers, already hit by the closure of the Channel Tunnel to all but freight trains after a fire last week. Some drivers wanting to cross to Britain drove to Belgian ports instead.

"The majority of refineries are blocked or have an uncertain situation," a spokeswoman for the oil industry association UFIP said. Only four of 13 were unaffected. About 100 of the 18,000 petrol stations had run out of fuel.
Authorities in the western town of Rennes ordered some 20 petrol stations to only supply emergency vehicles such as firemen and ambulances.
Carmaker Renault SA said it halted work at its Douai plant in northern France because of a lack of supplies.

The protests crept closer to Paris, with roadblocks at Elf Aquitaine's Grandpuits refinery and on roads to the wholesale food market. The main motorway north of the capital was briefly cut to one lane on the southbound carriage near Roissy airport.
The British government urged a quick end to the strike.
